desc: INSCOM is the United States Army's intelligence and security major command, headquartered in this period at Arlington Hall Station, Arlington, Virginia, with subordinate elements at Fort George G. Meade. Its own documents date its exploitation of psychoenergetics to Project GRILL FLAME in 1977, undertaken after the Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence and the commanding general agreed that INSCOM would check out the phenomenon and that Army Intelligence would obligate seventy-five thousand dollars for an SRI International selection and training programme. The successor project, CENTER LANE, was run from the Security Support Detachment of the 902d Military Intelligence Group at Fort George G. Meade under a special access programme designated by the Secretary of the Army, with a category-three access caveat on every page. INSCOM's commanding general recommended ending the Army's involvement in July 1984 and, on 2 March 1985, notified the Department of the Army of the project's deactivation and of the attachment of its assets and resources to the Defense Intelligence Agency under operational control. The command's 1977 establishment order has not been opened; the dateStart above is the year INSCOM's own memorandum gives for the start of the work, not for the command.

dossier.denialPosture: The board records no denial link on this node in either direction, and that is the point worth stating. INSCOM never had to deny CENTER LANE, because the access controls did the work a denial would otherwise have to do: a Secretary of the Army designated special access programme with a category three caveat on every page needs no public position at all. When the command was finished with it, it did not disown the project; it deactivated it, moved the assets to DIA under operational control and retired the nickname. The board treats the retirement of a nickname as a documented behaviour rather than an inference, because the letter that does it is in the file.
dossier.narrative:
The value of INSCOM to this board is that it settles by document what every other compartmented account has to argue by inference: that the United States has taken a subject the public conversation treats as absurd and run it at service-secretary access levels for the better part of a decade. The GDIP memorandum of 4 April 1984 says so in the command's own voice, dating the work and complaining about how it was funded in the same sentence: 'Since the beginning of USAINSCOM's exploitation of psychoenergetics (PE) technology with Project GRILL FLAME in 1977 through the present effort under CENTER LANE, the project has been conducted on an ad hoc basis, using resources taken "out of hide."' A programme paid for out of hide and controlled at category three is a precise description of the structure this board keeps asserting exists.

The origin is equally documented and equally ordinary. A 1978 talking paper records that 'ACSI & MG Rolya agreed that INSCOM would "check out" parapsychology phenomen[a], and that Army Intelligence would obligate $75 K to support an SRI Subject selection and training program for INSCOM personnel over the next year', with the contract let through AMSAA and the money buying a project manager and three subjects. The Army staff started it, the Army staff paid for it, and a nonprofit research institute in California supplied the method. That is the same shape the board traces at SRI International and later at BAASS: a government sponsor with deniability, a private research house with a security apparatus, and a small line of money.

What makes the ending as useful as the beginning is that INSCOM did not conceal the project so much as move it. The July 1984 memorandum has the commanding general writing that 'INSCOM ... should discontinue our involvement with psychoenergetic research and operations', intending 'to cease INSCOM CENTER LANE Project operations on 30 Sept 1984', and asking for authority to permit 'timely and undisrupted transfer of (1) ICLP operations to a national agency such as DIA or NSA'. The transfer happened. A capability judged not worth the Army's trouble was handed intact to a defence agency and its name retired, which is exactly how a programme becomes hard to follow without anyone destroying anything.
openQuestions: The command's 1977 establishment order has not been opened. The board's start date for this node is the year INSCOM's own memorandum gives for the start of the work, not for the command, and the record says so.

The CENTER LANE security classification guide is on the board's source list with eight pages exempt. What those eight pages withhold is the single most direct statement available about what the access categories were protecting, and it has not been obtained.
What DIA did with the assets and resources after 2 March 1985 is not established by anything opened for this node. The attachment is documented; the destination programme's own record is not.
dossier.whatItIs: The United States Army Intelligence and Security Command, the Army's intelligence and security major command, headquartered in the period the board covers at Arlington Hall Station, Arlington, Virginia, with subordinate elements at Fort George G. Meade. Its letterhead in this period reads 'DEPARTMENT OF THE ARMY / UNITED STATES ARMY INTELLIGENCE AND SECURITY COMMAND / ARLINGTON HALL STATION / ARLINGTON, VIRGINIA 22212'. From 1977 it ran the Army's psychoenergetics effort, first as Project GRILL FLAME and then as the INSCOM CENTER LANE Project, worked out of the Security Support Detachment of the 902d Military Intelligence Group at Fort Meade.
dossier.whyImplicated: INSCOM is the board's cleanest documented case of a ridiculed subject held inside the machinery of a special access programme, with the paperwork surviving to prove it. CENTER LANE was not an INSCOM designation. It was 'a Secretary of the Army designated Special Access Program', and every page of the project's file carries the caveat 'CENTER LANE SPECIAL ACCESS PROGRAM RESTRICT DISSEMINATION TO THOSE WITH VERIFIED ACCESS TO CATEGORY THREE (3)'. The command's own commanding general recommended ending the work, then on 2 March 1985 notified the Department of the Army of the deactivation, of the attachment of the project's assets and resources to the Defense Intelligence Agency under operational control, and of the retirement of the nickname. Start, funding, access control, termination and handoff are all in opened documents.
